# Characters of the subgroup generated by four actual powers

## Statement

Use the [local finite-orbit test](Yin_C_A0291_v1.md#statement) at the order-24 half-kernel.
For \(m\ge2\) write \(u_j=t_j^m\) for \(-1\le j\le2\), \(L_m=\langle u_{-1},u_0,u_1,u_2\rangle\), and
\[
                A_m=(L_m)_{\rm ab}/\langle\overline u_{-1},\overline u_2\rangle .
\]
Let \(r_m\) count the pairs \(0\le c,d<m\) with \(t_2^c g t_{-1}^d\in L_m\), where \(g=s^4\).
Then \(A_m\) is finite, each of \(\overline u_0,\overline u_1\) has order at most \(2r_m\) in it, and
\[
        |A_m|\le4r_m^2,\qquad
        1\le r_m\le m^2/\gcd(m,6).
\]
In particular the outer two power classes span the rational abelianization of \(L_m\).
For the ordinary subgroup generated by four squares, their index in the abelianization is at most sixteen, and each interior square has order at most four modulo the outer two.
If the zero Fourier block in the proof has a single nonzero finite pole in its power variable, each individual order bound improves to \(r_m\).
All characters used for this test are characters of the actual subgroup \(L_m\).

## The coefficient at the identity coset belongs to the subgroup

For the Fourier blocks of the transfer and its inverse as in the local test write
\[
             E_a(z)=z^a F_a(z^m),\qquad B_c(z)=z^c G_c(z^m).
\]
The rational matrices \(F_a,G_c\) exist because the fixed field of rotation by the \(m\)-th roots is \(\mathbb C(z^m)\).
In the [identity-coset matrix coefficient](Yin_C_A0291_v1.md#local-fourier-blocks-and-separation-of-repeated-endpoints) put \(\ell_{ab}=t_1^a t_0^b\), \(k_{cd}=t_2^c g t_{-1}^d\).
On its left, commute the first power-variable function to the left edge and the second to the right edge of the product.
On its right use \(t_3^m g=g t_{-1}^m\) to move the last function across \(g\).
The identity reads
\[
 \sum_{\ell_{ab}\in L_m} F_a(u_1)\ell_{ab}F_b(u_0)
     =\sum_{k_{cd}\in L_m}G_c(u_2) k_{cd} G_d(u_{-1}).
\]
All terms now lie in \(M_2(U(L_m))\); the regular inclusion into \(U(F)\) is injective.
The right side has at most \(r_m\) terms.
The bounds on \(r_m\) follow from the existence of a right match and the degree congruence in the [four-power test](Yin_C_A0291_v1.md#four-powers-and-the-identity-coset).

Given any circle character \(\chi\) of \(A_m\), use it on \(L_m\) by the displayed quotient.
Its regular unitary twist gives another identity in \(U(L_m)\).
The right-hand factors in the power variables are fixed since \(\chi(u_{-1})=\chi(u_2)=1\).
Only the scalars \(\chi(k_{cd})\) change there.
Consequently all twisted left sides lie in one complex vector space of dimension at most \(r_m\).

## Bidegree zero retains the moving poles

Use the [injective linear two-variable map](Yin_C_A0291_v1.md#local-fourier-blocks-and-separation-of-repeated-endpoints) for the neighboring cyclics \(t_1,t_0\), entrywise.
The twisted left side is the image of the matrix of separated rational tensors
\[
    \sum_{\ell_{ab}\in L_m}\chi(\ell_{ab})\,
         z^a F_a(\chi(u_1)z^m)\,{z'}^b F_b(\chi(u_0){z'}^m).
\]
The span of these tensors still has dimension at most \(r_m\) by injectivity.
Average independently over \(m\)-th-root rotations in \(z,z'\).
This kills every index pair except \((0,0)\), which occurs with \(\ell_{00}=1\).
On putting \(X=z^m,Y={z'}^m\) the following family of rational matrices therefore spans a space of dimension at most \(r_m\):
\[
                  F_0(\chi(u_1)X)F_0(\chi(u_0)Y),
                                  \qquad \chi\in\widehat A_m .
\]
This use of independent rotations is on separated formal tensors after pulling back the identities; the group has supplied only the actual characters of \(L_m\).

The rational matrix \(F_0(X)\) is invertible by the [zero-frequency corner calculations](Yin_C_A0291_v1.md#four-powers-and-the-identity-coset).
Its nonzero finite pole set \(\mathcal P\) is nonempty and has at most two elements.
To check this when \(D\) is invertible, use \(T=D^{-1}C,\ V=A-BT\) in the [transfer expansion](Yin_C_A0280_v1.md#which-finite-frequencies-must-contribute).
The zero component of \(M(z)=BD^{-1}+Vz(I+zT)^{-1}D^{-1}\) is
\[
     F_0(X)=BD^{-1}
             +(-1)^{m-1}VX T^{m-1}(I-(-1)^m X T^m)^{-1}D^{-1}.
\]
The matrix \(V\) is invertible.
The determinant of the denominator pencil has a circle zero, so \(T\) has a nonzero eigenvalue \(\lambda\).
Apply the formula to \(D\) times an eigenvector at \(\lambda\).
The second term has a genuine pole at \(X=(-1)^m\lambda^{-m}\) with nonzero numerator there.
All possible nonzero finite poles arise from the at most two nonzero eigenvalues.
If \(D\) is singular then \(C\) is invertible.
Apply the same argument to the transfer at \(z^{-1}\); its zero-index block replaces \(X\) by \(X^{-1}\), preserving the count and nonemptiness.

For fixed \(\chi\) the poles of the product in \(X\), over the coefficient field \(\mathbb C(Y)\), are exactly \(\chi(u_1)^{-1}\mathcal P\) among nonzero finite points.
The second factor is invertible over that field and hence cannot cancel a pole.
The identical statement holds in \(Y\) by invertibility of the first factor.
A basis selected from the family has at most \(r_m\) members.
Every nonzero finite \(X\)-pole anywhere in its span must already occur among the basis pole sets.
Following a single member of \(\mathcal P\) through the \(\chi(u_1)^{-1}\) rotations shows that the number of distinct \(\chi(u_1)\) is at most \(|\mathcal P|r_m\); apply the \(Y\) argument to \(u_0\).
In a finitely generated abelian group an element of infinite order has infinitely many circle-character values, and one of finite order \(n\) has exactly \(n\) such values by the structure theorem.
The two bounds follow; the two interior classes generate \(A_m\), giving the order and index assertions.
